```{r echo=FALSE, include=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# all library load statements here
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)

r.version <- "4.3.2"
seed.val <- 123456

# Descriptive statistics table for a numeric variable, rounded to the hundredth
desc.tbl <- function(x) {
  q <- as.numeric(quantile(x))
  statistic <- c("Min", "1st Quant. (25%)", "Mean", "Median",
                 "3rd Quant. (75%)", "Max", "StdDev")
  value <- sprintf("%.2f", c(min(x), q[2], mean(x), median(x), q[4], max(x), sd(x)))
  data.frame(statistic, value)
}

# Counts and percentages for a categorical variable
count.tbl <- function(x) {
  tb <- table(x)
  data.frame(Level = names(tb), Count = as.integer(tb),
             Percent = sprintf("%.2f", 100 * as.numeric(tb) / sum(tb)))
}
```

# Overview

How far a car can go on a gallon of gas affects how much the owner spends on fuel and how much the car pollutes, so fuel economy is something both buyers and car makers pay close attention to. Car makers have to balance it against other things buyers want, like more power and a bigger car. A car with more horsepower usually has a bigger engine that burns more fuel, so we would expect it to get fewer miles per gallon. But horsepower usually goes up together with the car's weight, the size of the engine (displacement) and the number of cylinders, so it is hard to tell how much of the drop in fuel economy comes from horsepower itself and how much comes from the car just being bigger and heavier.

In this analysis we look at cars from model years 1970 to 1982. This was a time when gas prices went up sharply and car makers started building smaller and more efficient cars, so there is a wide range of cars in the data, from small four cylinder cars to large cars with eight cylinder engines.

The main research question of this analysis is: to what extent does horsepower influence a vehicle's fuel efficiency, and how does its predictive importance compare with vehicle weight, engine displacement, and number of cylinders?

# Data Description and Processing

The data set used in this analysis is the Auto MPG data set from the UCI Machine Learning Repository [1]. It was originally taken from the StatLib library at Carnegie Mellon University, and it has the fuel economy and specifications of 398 cars from model years 1970 to 1982. Since our research question compares horsepower with weight, displacement and cylinders, we grouped those four variables together as size and power variables, and grouped the rest as other vehicle variables: \

Size and Power Variables: \
horsepower: Engine horsepower. numeric \
weight: Weight of the car in pounds. numeric \
displacement: Engine displacement (size of the engine) in cubic inches. numeric \
cylinders: Number of cylinders in the engine (3, 4, 5, 6 or 8). numeric \
\par
Other Vehicle Variables: \
acceleration: Time it takes the car to accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in seconds. numeric \
model_year: Model year of the car, recorded as the last two digits (70 = 1970 through 82 = 1982). numeric \
origin: Region where the car was made. categorical: usa, europe or japan \
name: Make and model name of the car, for example "ford pinto". categorical \
\par
Outcome: \
mpg: Fuel economy of the car in miles per gallon. numeric \

The dependent variable is mpg and the other variables are the independent variables. In the original data, origin is recorded as 1, 2 and 3, so we converted these to usa, europe and japan to make the results easier to read. The name variable has 301 different values, so almost every car has its own level. We did not include name as a predictor, since it only identifies the car and would add hundreds of levels to a model without telling us anything about fuel economy. This leaves seven predictors.

The data set was checked for missing values. Of the original 398 observations, 6 cars were missing a value for horsepower. Since horsepower is the main predictor in our research question, we removed these 6 observations instead of filling them in, leaving 392 complete observations. We also checked the numeric variables for extreme outliers using the outer fences (more than 3 times the interquartile range below the first quartile or above the third quartile). None of the values fell outside the outer fences, so we did not remove any outliers.

```{r echo=FALSE}
# the data file has no header, values are separated by spaces and missing values are "?"
data.df <- read.table("auto-mpg.data", na.strings = "?",
                      col.names = c("mpg", "cylinders", "displacement", "horsepower",
                                    "weight", "acceleration", "model_year", "origin", "name"))
data.df <- na.omit(data.df)
data.df$origin <- factor(data.df$origin, levels = c(1, 2, 3),
                         labels = c("usa", "europe", "japan"))
```

# Data Exploration

The distribution of the outcome variable, fuel economy in miles per gallon, is shown in figure 1. It is slightly right-skewed: most cars get between about 15 and 30 miles per gallon, with the most common values between 15 and 20, and a smaller number of very efficient cars stretching the tail out past 40 miles per gallon.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Distribution of fuel economy (miles per gallon).", fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5, fig.align="center"}
hist(data.df$mpg, freq = FALSE, breaks = 15,
     main = "", xlab = "Fuel economy (miles per gallon)", ylab = "Density")
lines(density(data.df$mpg), lwd = 2)
```

The descriptive statistics are in table 1. The mean of 23.45 miles per gallon is a little above the median of 22.75. Fuel economy ranges from 9 to 46.6 miles per gallon, and the standard deviation is 7.81.

```{r echo=FALSE}
kable(desc.tbl(data.df$mpg),
      caption = "Fuel economy descriptive statistics (miles per gallon)")
```

The skew is fairly mild, so we do not expect it to be a big problem for linear regression with a sample of 392 cars. We will still check the residuals of our fitted models for any patterns or non-constant variance.

# Modeling

To answer our research question, we plan to use two models:

1. Multiple linear regression. We will fit a model with mpg as the dependent variable and all seven predictors as the independent variables, with origin included as a dummy variable and usa as the baseline. We will use the coefficients and p-values to compare the importance of horsepower with weight, displacement and cylinders, and the adjusted R-squared to describe the overall fit. Since the four size and power variables tend to go up together, we will also calculate the variance inflation factor (VIF) for each predictor to check for multicollinearity.

2. Decision tree. We will fit a regression tree with the same dependent variable and predictors. A tree does not assume a straight-line relationship between the predictors and mpg, and its variable importance values give a second way to rank horsepower against the other size and power variables.

To compare how well the two models predict fuel economy for cars they have not seen, we will use repeated 10-fold cross validation and compare the average root mean squared error (RMSE) of each model.

# References

[1] Quinlan, R. (1993). Auto MPG [Data set]. UCI Machine Learning Repository. https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/9/auto+mpg
